newsitem.title: GERMANY: Institute adds to German doubts on EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Institute adds to German doubts on EMU start.

text.p: Germany's budget deficit will overshoot European monetary union targets abd reach 3.25 percent of economic output, a research body said on Monday, adding to rising speculation that EMU will be delayed.

The HWWA institute in Hamburg predicted the German economy would grow 2.5 percent in 1997, in line with Bonn's estimate. It also forecast an average unemployment rate of 10.8 percent -- equivalent to 4.15 million workers and just under the Bonn government's forecast of 4.2 million.

But without a stronger economic turnaround, Germany is at risk of missing a key requirement for European economic and monetary union -- total public sector deficit of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, the institute said.
"All things considered, the economy in Germany will display no great impetus this year," the HWWA said. "Under these conditions, a clear recovery in the job market is not to be expected."

HWWA, one of six independent bodies whose estimates are used by Bonn, said it expected the European Union to adopt a loose interpretation of entry criteria to allow EMU to go ahead in 1999 as planned.
"Under a strict interpretation, only a few countries will fulfil the entry criteria, so that a delay of the start of EMU would be conceivable," HWWA said.
"More likely than a delay to the starting date is, however, that the criteria will be interpreted more generously for political reasons, despite vehement claims to the contrary."

The HWWA report came after Herbert Hax, a leading German economist, called for a delay in the EMU start date. Over the weekend he said Bonn would likely miss the deficit target and the requirement for government debt of under 60 percent of GDP.
Hax, one of the "five wisemen" who advise the government, told a German newspaper Bonn should put off joining a single currency until its own finances were in order.

On Monday Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said he doubted Bonn could meet its prediction of deficits of 2.9 percent of GDP. But he stopped short of suggesting an EMU delay, saying that would deal a major setback to government efforts to consolidate budgets.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday maintained Germany would fulfil convergence criteria for EMU and that the common currency would be launched in 1999.
